# Corsair

> Every written page of https://docs.corsair.dev, as Markdown, in sidebar order. The ~2,500 per-plugin pages are left out: a plugin's pages are at https://docs.corsair.dev/plugins/<id>/overview.md, /api.md, /database.md, /webhooks.md and /get-credentials.md, and the plugin list is at https://docs.corsair.dev/guides/plugins.md. The changelog is at https://docs.corsair.dev/changelog.md. The index of every page is https://docs.corsair.dev/llms.txt.

Generated from docs/ by `pnpm generate:llms-full`; don't edit by hand.

# Introduction

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/introduction.md

> Open-source integration layer for agents and apps.

Corsair is an open-source integration layer for apps and agents. Connect to GitHub, Slack, Gmail, and 200+ other services through one syntax. Corsair handles OAuth, token refresh, webhooks, and rate limits.

You run it inside your own app. Credentials stay encrypted in your database. [Hub](https://docs.corsair.dev/hub/overview.md) hosts connect pages and OAuth callbacks so you don't build those public URLs yourself.

Install plugins, wire up Corsair once, then call any integration the same way:

```ts corsair.ts
import { createCorsair } from 'corsair';
import { github } from '@corsair-dev/github';
import { slack } from '@corsair-dev/slack';

export const corsair = createCorsair({
  plugins: [github(), slack()],
  database: db,
  kek: process.env.CORSAIR_KEK!,
  hub: {
    projectApiKey: process.env.CORSAIR_API_KEY!,
    signingSecret: process.env.CORSAIR_SIGNING_SECRET!,
  },
});
```

```ts route.ts
await corsair.github.api.issues.create({ owner: 'acme', repo: 'app', title: 'Bug' });
await corsair.slack.api.messages.post({ channel: 'C123', text: 'On it.' });
```

## Get started

- [Quick start](https://docs.corsair.dev/quick-start.md): Empty project to a connected integration in five steps.

* [Set up with your agent](https://docs.corsair.dev/getting-started/set-up-with-your-agent.md): One prompt for your coding agent to wire Corsair in.

- [Pick your framework](https://docs.corsair.dev/frameworks/next.md): Next, Node, Express, Hono, SvelteKit, Remix, Astro. Mount the route in yours.

* [Browse plugins](https://docs.corsair.dev/guides/plugins.md): Slack, Linear, Gmail, GitHub, HubSpot, Stripe, and hundreds more.

# Quick start

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/quick-start.md

> A working integration in five steps, powered by Hub.

Hub hosts the OAuth connect, approval, and webhook surfaces, so there are no connect pages, callback routes, or per-environment redirect URIs to build. Credentials are encrypted and stored in your own database. Hub stores none.

```bash Set up with your agent
npx skills add https://github.com/corsairdev/corsair --skill corsair
```

**Step 1**

## Install

```bash npm
npm install corsair @corsair-dev/github
```

```bash yarn
yarn add corsair @corsair-dev/github
```

```bash pnpm
pnpm install corsair @corsair-dev/github
```

```bash bun
bun add corsair @corsair-dev/github
```

> [!TIP]
>
> `@corsair-dev/github` is one plugin. Every service is its own `@corsair-dev/*` package. Find the one you need, and its exact install id, in the [**Plugins**](https://docs.corsair.dev/guides/plugins.md) catalog.

**Step 2**

## Set your environment

Create a project in the [Hub dashboard](https://hub.corsair.dev/dashboard) and copy the **development** API key and signing secret. Then generate a KEK. Corsair encrypts every stored credential with it:

```bash
openssl rand -base64 32
```

```bash .env
CORSAIR_KEK=your-generated-kek
CORSAIR_API_KEY=ck_dev_...
CORSAIR_SIGNING_SECRET=...
```

> [!WARNING]
>
> Keep your KEK safe. Lose it and you lose access to every stored credential. Treat it like a root password.

**Step 3**

## Create the database

Corsair stores data in five tables. SQLite is the fastest way to start:

```bash npm
npm install better-sqlite3
```

```bash yarn
yarn add better-sqlite3
```

```bash pnpm
pnpm install better-sqlite3
```

```bash bun
bun add better-sqlite3
```

**View migration SQL**

```sql migration.sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS corsair_integrations (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    config TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    dek TEXT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS corsair_accounts (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    integration_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    config TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    dek TEXT NULL,
    FOREIGN KEY (integration_id) REFERENCES corsair_integrations(id)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS corsair_entities (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    entity_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    entity_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    version TEXT NOT NULL,
    data TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES corsair_accounts(id)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS corsair_events (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    account_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    event_type TEXT NOT NULL,
    payload TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    status TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES corsair_accounts(id)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS corsair_permissions (
    id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    token TEXT NOT NULL,
    plugin TEXT NOT NULL,
    endpoint TEXT NOT NULL,
    args TEXT NOT NULL,
    tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
    status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
    expires_at TEXT NOT NULL,
    error TEXT
);
```

**macOS / Linux**

```bash
sqlite3 corsair.db < migration.sql
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**

> [!NOTE]
>
> **PowerShell syntax**: Bash redirection and $VAR env vars do not work in PowerShell. Use the Windows commands shown in this tab instead.

```powershell
Get-Content migration.sql | sqlite3 corsair.db
```

Using Postgres, Drizzle, or Prisma instead? See [Database](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md) for each option.

**Step 4**

## Configure Corsair

Wire your database, KEK, and Hub keys together in `src/server/corsair.ts`:

```ts src/server/corsair.ts
import Database from 'better-sqlite3';
import { createCorsair } from 'corsair';
import { github } from '@corsair-dev/github';

const db = new Database('corsair.db');

export const corsair = createCorsair({
    plugins: [github({ authType: 'managed' })],
    database: db,
    kek: process.env.CORSAIR_KEK!,
    multiTenancy: true, // gives every user their own credentials; enables corsair.withTenant(id)
    hub: {
        projectApiKey: process.env.CORSAIR_API_KEY!,
        signingSecret: process.env.CORSAIR_SIGNING_SECRET!,
    },
});
```

Mount the handler once. It serves Hub delivery and the management API. In development, Hub auto-detects your localhost delivery URL:

```ts app/api/corsair/[[...path]]/route.ts
import { toNextJsHandler } from 'corsair';
import { corsair } from '@/server/corsair';

export const { GET, POST, OPTIONS } = toNextJsHandler(corsair, {
    basePath: '/api/corsair',
});
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> This quick-start uses Next.js. The instance above is the same on every framework; only the mount line changes. See [Frameworks](https://docs.corsair.dev/frameworks/next.md) for Express, Node, SvelteKit, Hono, and the rest.

Add more plugins later, like `slack()`, `linear()`, or `gmail()`, by appending to the array.

**Step 5**

## Connect and call

Mint a connect link and send the user to it. Hub hosts the connect page and delivers the result back to your app, with no connect page or OAuth callback to build:

```ts connect.ts
const { connectUrl } = await corsair.manage.connect.createLink({
    plugin: 'github',
    tenantId: 'acme',
});
// redirect the user's browser to connectUrl
```

Once connected, call any endpoint. Responses are also cached in your database for instant reads:

```ts usage.ts
const repos = await corsair.github.api.repositories.list({});
```

Want an agent to call endpoints on its own? See [MCP Adapters](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/mcp-adapters.md).

**Step 6**

## Run it

```bash
npm run dev
```

Load your app so the mounted route gets its first hit. That request registers your delivery URL with Hub, and the **App sync** dot in the dashboard header turns green. A green dot means Hub can reach your app and the connect flow is live.

## What's next

- [Use with AI](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/mcp-adapters.md): Give an agent the three Corsair tools and let it discover and call any endpoint.

* [Hub overview](https://docs.corsair.dev/hub/overview.md): How the relay works, and why Hub stores none of your credentials.

- [Environments](https://docs.corsair.dev/hub/environments.md): Development vs production keys. Switch to production when you deploy.

* [Multi-tenancy](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/multi-tenancy.md): Building a product? Flip one flag and every user gets their own data and credentials.

- [Database options](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md): Postgres, Drizzle, Prisma, and the five tables Corsair uses.

* [Provisioning](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/provisioning.md): Seed credentials and provision tenants from the `corsair` CLI or `setupCorsair`.

---

# Corsair Cloud

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/overview.md

> A hosted runtime for your integrations. You have an API key, and every tool call is one HTTP request.

Corsair Cloud runs the integration layer for you. Instead of building and
hosting a server that talks to Notion, Slack, GitHub, and the rest, you get a
project with its own hosted runtime and call any plugin operation over HTTP.

Nothing to deploy, no OAuth server to write, no tokens to store. Connect your
users' accounts once, then make calls.

## Set up

You need one thing: your project's **API key**, from the dashboard Overview
page. It looks like `ck_cloud_…`. The client derives its own URL from the key,
so that's the whole configuration.

> [!WARNING]
>
> The API key is a server secret, sent as a bearer token. Keep it on your
> server; never put it in browser code or a mobile app you ship. For the browser,
> see [Server vs. browser](#server-vs-browser).

## Your first call

Install the client for your language and make one call. Every language takes the
key and nothing else.

```ts TypeScript
import { corsairCloud } from "corsair";

const corsair = corsairCloud({ apiKey: process.env.CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY! });

const pages = await corsair.withTenant("acme").notion.api.pages.searchPage({});
```

```python Python
from corsair_cloud import CorsairCloud
import os

corsair = CorsairCloud(api_key=os.environ["CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY"])

pages = corsair.with_tenant("acme").call("notion", "pages.searchPage", {})
```

```go Go
corsair := corsaircloud.New(os.Getenv("CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY"))

raw, err := corsair.Tenant("acme").Call(ctx, "notion", "pages.searchPage", map[string]any{})
```

```swift Swift
let corsair = CorsairCloud(apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY"]!)

let pages = try await corsair.tenant("acme").call("notion", "pages.searchPage", args: [:])
```

```bash curl
# The clients derive the URL from the key; for raw curl, build it from your key's
# slug (the segment between ck_cloud_ and the first '.'): https://api.corsair.cloud/<slug>/api/corsair
curl -X POST "https://api.corsair.cloud/<slug>/api/corsair/acme/notion/call/pages.searchPage" \
  -H "authorization: Bearer $CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"args":{}}'
```

That runs Notion's `pages.searchPage` as your user "acme" and returns the
result. It's always one request, `POST /{tenant}/{plugin}/call/{op}` with a
`{ "args": {...} }` body, so the language clients are thin wrappers over the
same shape.

## What is a tenant?

A tenant is one of your users. `withTenant("acme")` (or `with_tenant`, `Tenant`,
`tenant`) picks which user a call acts as, so it uses that user's connected
account. One runtime serves all your tenants at once. Building for a single
user? Pick one tenant id and forget about it.

The runtime rejects an empty tenant id rather than guessing, so a call is never
silently scoped to the wrong user.

## Map your tenants

The runtime holds the tenants and which accounts each has connected. List them
to line up against your own users:

```ts TypeScript
const tenants = await corsair.manage.tenants.list();
// [{ id: "acme", connectedPlugins: ["notion"] }, …]
```

```python Python
tenants = corsair.manage.tenants()
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> `tenants` gives you each tenant's id and connected plugins, `connectionStatus`
> gives the per-plugin auth state, and `manage.permissions.get({ id })` reads a
> permission grant (its scopes and approval status). All redact secrets: you see
> *that* a tenant connected Notion, never their token. Reading a tenant's stored
> *data* rows directly, or pointing the runtime at your own database, comes with
> bring-your-own-DB (coming soon).

## Connect a user's account

Before a tenant can call Notion, they have to connect their Notion account.
Corsair Cloud runs the OAuth. Create a connect link and send your user to it:

```ts TypeScript
const link = await corsair.manage.connect.createLink({
  plugin: "notion",
  tenantId: "acme",
});
// send the user to link.connectUrl
```

```python Python
link = corsair.manage.create_connect_link("notion", "acme")
# send the user to link["connectUrl"]
```

When they finish authorizing, the runtime stores their token, encrypted at rest
with a key Corsair holds. Raw provider tokens never sit in your store. Check who
is connected any time:

```ts TypeScript
const status = await corsair.manage.connectionStatus.get({ tenantId: "acme" });
// { notion: "connected" }
```

```python Python
status = corsair.manage.connection_status("acme")
# {"notion": "connected"}
```

## Server vs. browser

The runtime has one contract and two ways to reach it:

- **From a server or agent.** Use the client directly. It holds the key and
  calls the runtime, the path in every example above.
- **From a browser (React).** Browser code must never see the key. Stand up a
  route in *your own* app that injects the bearer server-side. `corsair/connect`
  builds that route from just the key:

```ts app/api/corsair/[...path]/route.ts
import { corsairConnect } from 'corsair/connect';
import { getSession } from '@/lib/auth';

const proxy = corsairConnect({
    apiKey: process.env.CORSAIR_CLOUD_KEY!,
    // Runs before every forwarded request. The caller's own credentials
    // never reach this handler, so this is where you check who's asking.
    authorize: async (req) => Boolean(await getSession(req)),
});

export const GET = proxy;
export const POST = proxy;
```

Pair it with `<CorsairProvider baseURL="/api/corsair">` in the browser. The
provider only ever calls this same-origin route and never sees the key.

`authorize` is required: without it, `corsairConnect` throws at startup, since
anyone who can reach the route could otherwise invoke any tenant/plugin/operation
the project key allows. To intentionally run an open proxy, pass
`allowUnauthenticated: true`.

Then wrap your app in `CorsairProvider` and use `useCorsair()` to drive the
connect flow and read connection state. The key stays on your server the whole
time.

## Type hints for your calls (TypeScript)

`corsairCloud` takes no plugin list, since the plugins live on the runtime, so
by default `corsair.withTenant(t).notion.api…` is typed as `any`. For
autocomplete, run the CLI once:

```bash
pnpm corsair cloud pull
```

It reads the exact plugins and operations your runtime has, down to the scopes
you allowed, and writes a local `corsair-env.d.ts` that TypeScript picks up, with
no plugin import to maintain. Coding agents can skip it and list operations with
`pnpm corsair cloud list`.

## Where calls go

Your call goes straight to the runtime, not through the dashboard. The dashboard
creates and configures the runtime, then steps out of the request path, so a
call is one hop out (your code to the runtime) and one hop on (the runtime to the
provider).

## Next steps

- [Python client](https://docs.corsair.dev/clients/python.md)
- [Go client](https://docs.corsair.dev/clients/go.md)
- [Swift client](https://docs.corsair.dev/clients/swift.md)

# Corsair MCP

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/mcp.md

> One address, https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp, that lets Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor and other agents use the apps you've connected to Corsair.

Corsair MCP lets an AI agent use the apps you've connected to Corsair. It can read your inbox, post in Slack, open a GitHub issue, search data Corsair has synced, hand a file to one of your apps, or set up an automation that runs when something happens in one of your apps.

Every client uses the same address:

```
https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp
```

You add it once, sign in to Corsair, and choose which of your links the client uses.

## Before you start

- A Corsair account. Sign up at [hub.corsair.dev](https://hub.corsair.dev) with Google, GitHub or an emailed sign-in link.
- Apps to use. You can connect them in Corsair first, or ask the agent to connect one later. It hands you a sign-in link for that app.

## How sign-in works

**Step 1**

### Add the address to your client

See [Add it to your client](#add-it-to-your-client) below.

**Step 2**

### Sign in to Corsair

The client opens Corsair in your browser.

**Step 3**

### Pick a link

A link is a set of your connected apps plus a [mode](#modes-and-approvals) that decides what the agent may do without asking. Pick an existing link or make a new one for this client. If you have no link yet, Corsair asks you to make one first.

**Step 4**

### Allow

The client gets the apps on that link and your email address. Nothing else on your account is shared.

One connection uses one link. To switch links, remove Corsair from the client, add it again and pick the other link. You can sign a client out of a link at any time from [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me).

## Add it to your client

**Claude**

1. In Claude, open **Plugins**, select **Add**, then **Add custom connector**.
2. Name it Corsair, paste `https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp` and select **Continue**.
3. Keep the settings Claude detects and select **Add**, then sign in to Corsair.

On a Team or Enterprise plan, an owner adds connectors under Organization settings.

**ChatGPT**

1. In ChatGPT, add a custom MCP server and paste `https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp`.
2. Choose OAuth, then sign in to Corsair.

On personal plans, ChatGPT currently uses only the read tools from a custom server, so Corsair can look things up but not make changes. Write tools such as `run_script` need a Business or Enterprise/Edu workspace, where an admin adds the server or gives you permission to. OpenAI's [guide to custom MCP servers](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12584461-connecting-custom-mcp-servers-in-chatgpt) has the current rules.

**Cursor**

[Add to Cursor](cursor://anysphere.cursor-deeplink/mcp/install?name=corsair\&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwczovL21jcC5jb3JzYWlyLmRldi9tY3AifQ==), or add this to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "corsair": { "url": "https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp" }
  }
}
```

Cursor opens Corsair to sign in the first time it connects.

**VS Code**

Add this to `.vscode/mcp.json`, or run **MCP: Add Server → HTTP** and paste the address:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "corsair": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp" }
  }
}
```

VS Code signs you in when it first connects.

**Claude Code**

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http corsair https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp
```

Then run `/mcp` in Claude Code to sign in. Add `--scope user` to have it in every project.

**Codex**

```bash
codex mcp add corsair --url https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp
```

Codex usually opens Corsair to sign in as soon as you add it. If it says the server may or may not require login instead, or you need to sign in again later, run `codex mcp login corsair`.

**Gemini CLI**

```bash
gemini mcp add --transport http corsair https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp
```

Then run `/mcp auth corsair` to sign in.

**Zed**

Add this to your Zed settings. Zed signs you in when it first connects.

```json
{
  "context_servers": {
    "corsair": { "url": "https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp" }
  }
}
```

Any other client that supports remote MCP servers with OAuth sign-in works the same way.

> [!NOTE]
>
> Some clients can't sign in to an MCP server, such as GitHub Copilot's coding agent. For those, use a link's own address with an API key. Open the link at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me) and follow the steps for your client there.

## What the agent can do

| Tool                | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Type            |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
| `list_integrations` | Lists the apps on this link, whether each is ready and which account it's signed in as, with the Corsair credits left and spent this month. Also checks whether Corsair can connect an app that isn't here yet                                                                                                                                                | Read            |
| `get_connect_link`  | Returns the sign-in link for an app, adding the app first if it isn't here. Apps that run on Corsair's own account come back ready, with no link. Shows a [connect card](#cards) where the chat supports it                                                                                                                                                   | Write           |
| `list_operations`   | Shows what connected apps can do, with each action's risk and price. Searched by what you want to do, it returns the matching actions with the arguments they require                                                                                                                                                                                         | Read            |
| `get_schema`        | Shows the full arguments and return shape of one or more actions                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Read            |
| `search`            | Answers a question about your data, usually in one call: Corsair's own PM, CRM, routines and files, and the email, chat, issues, docs and calendars of your connected apps. When an app's synced copy is behind, it reads that app live. When nothing matches, it says so instead of offering the closest records as an answer. It also opens results in full | Read            |
| `read_data`         | Reads your apps live with a short script, for what `search` doesn't have or what must be current. It stops before any action that would change something                                                                                                                                                                                                      | Read            |
| `run_script`        | Makes changes in your apps with a short script: send, create, update or delete                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Sensitive write |
| `get_job`           | Waits for a [long job](#long-jobs) a script started, such as a crawl or a document parse, and returns its result. Shows a [job card](#cards) where the chat supports it                                                                                                                                                                                       | Read            |
| `upload_file`       | Adds a file to your [Files](#files) so your apps can use it: a file you attached in the chat, a public URL or a file on your computer. With none of these, it gives you a link to pick the file. It only adds files and never replaces one. Shows an [upload card](#cards) where the chat supports it                                                         | Write           |
| `view_routines`     | Lists the routines on this link and their recent runs, or shows one run step by step with its error                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Read            |
| `update_routine`    | Creates, changes, pauses or removes a routine, an automation that runs on an app event or a schedule. Describe it in plain words and Corsair writes and tests it                                                                                                                                                                                              | Sensitive write |
| `use_skill`         | Loads one of your saved [skills](#skills) by name: its `SKILL.md`, then any file that comes with it                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Read            |
| `find_skill`        | Searches the public [skills.sh](https://skills.sh) directory for skills you haven't saved yet. Shows a [skills card](#cards) where the chat supports it                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Read            |
| `save_skill`        | Saves a skill for every agent on your link, from text, a GitHub URL or a skills.sh id. For a folder on your computer, such as `~/.claude/skills`, it gives you one command that uploads it                                                                                                                                                                    | Write           |
| `submit_feedback`   | Sends the Corsair team a short note about Corsair itself. The agent sends one on its own when Corsair lacks an app or action you asked for, or when a reply says the fault is on Corsair's side, and tells you it did. For a wrong or confusing answer it asks you first. A note never includes your app data                                                 | Write           |

Read tools never change anything in your apps. A read can still use [credits](#corsair-credits): `read_data` on an app that runs on Corsair's account is billed like any other call there. Write tools change only your Corsair setup and files, which you can undo, or send Corsair a note. Sensitive writes act in your apps, or set up a routine that will act later without asking, so a client should ask you before every call.

Scripts run in a sandbox that can only call your connected apps' actions. They have no network, filesystem or other system access, and the agent never sees your app credentials.

Not every link shows every tool. A link that isn't allowed to add apps has no `get_connect_link`, and a link that can't change routines has no `update_routine`. The skill tools come on the links you make at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me), and a link in Read mode has no `save_skill`.

`list_integrations`, `list_operations`, `get_schema`, `search`, `read_data`, `get_job`, `view_routines`, `use_skill` and `find_skill` are marked read-only, so most clients run them without asking. Clients usually ask you before running the others.

## Long jobs

Some actions start work that takes longer than one call: a site crawl, an async document parse, an agent run, an image or video prediction. Corsair notices when a script starts one and waits a few seconds. If the job finishes in that time, the result comes back with the script's. If not, the reply names the job, and the agent calls `get_job` to wait for it and get the result. The reply also gives a line to stop the job, where the app has one.

This works whether the app is connected with your own account or runs on Corsair's.

## Files

Every link has Files, where Corsair keeps files for your apps to use, up to 25 MB each. A script can't carry a file itself, so the agent first adds the file with `upload_file`, then passes its id (`fil_…`) to the app. Corsair gives the app a short-lived link to the file in its place.

How a file gets in depends on where you're chatting:

- **ChatGPT.** A file you attach goes straight to Files.
- **Claude.** The agent sends a file you attached from its code sandbox with one command. That needs the sandbox to reach Corsair: in claude.ai, add `auth.corsair.dev` under **Settings > Capabilities > Allowed websites**. Until you do, you pick the file in the upload card instead.
- **An agent with a shell**, such as Claude Code or Codex, sends a file from your computer with one command. The file goes straight to Corsair without passing through the chat.
- **Anywhere else**, you pick the file in the upload card, or on the upload page its link opens. The link works for 10 minutes.
- **A public URL**: Corsair fetches it.

`upload_file` only adds files, and sending the same file twice keeps one copy. A file is private to the link that added it until you share it with your workspace. In a script, the agent can read text files and the text of PDFs, change part of a text file, and save an app's output, such as a filled-in PDF, as a new file or a new version of one. Search finds files by name, and by what they say when they have text.

See, share and delete your files on your link's **Files** page: open the link at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me).

## Corsair's own apps

Besides the apps you connect, the agent can use apps that Corsair runs itself. They need no other account.

- **PM**: issues and projects, with a status, priority, assignee, labels and a due date.
- **CRM**: people, companies and deals, with notes and tasks.
- **pg**: your own Postgres databases, queried by name. See [Postgres databases](#postgres-databases).
- **Files**: files your apps can use. See [Files](#files).
- **Mate**: the chat assistant in Corsair. The agent can find and read your Mate chats, including ones in Shared.

Each one has a page on your link at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me).

### Postgres databases

pg lets the agent run SQL on your own Postgres databases without ever seeing their connection URLs.

- **Adding a database.** Ask the agent to add one, and it gives you a setup link. The workspace owner opens it within 30 minutes and pastes the connection URL there. Corsair stores the URL encrypted; it never passes through the chat.
- **Reading and writing.** The agent runs one statement at a time. A read runs in a transaction that is always rolled back, so nothing it does persists, and returns up to 1,000 rows. A write commits, and needs write access. A database marked read-only takes reads only, for everyone.
- **Access.** The owner chooses which teammates can read or write each database on the link's **pg** page, and its **Audit** tab lists every query.
- **Limits.** Per database: 10 queries per 10 seconds and 60 per minute for each person, and 120 per minute for everyone together.

## Skills

A skill is a set of instructions an agent loads when a task calls for it: a `SKILL.md`, sometimes with files it refers to. Save a skill to Corsair once and every agent on the same link can use it, in whichever client it runs. Corsair keeps your skills in your own Corsair instance.

- **Use one.** Each agent sees the list of your skills when it connects, and loads one with `use_skill` when a task matches it. Clients that show MCP prompts also list each skill as a prompt.
- **Find one.** Ask the agent for a skill, such as "find me a skill for writing PR descriptions". It searches skills.sh with `find_skill`, and you pick the one to add.
- **Save one.** Ask the agent to save a skill you wrote together in the chat, or one from GitHub or skills.sh. Saving your own skill again under the same name adds a new version.
- **Upload your own.** To add the skills you keep on your computer, such as `~/.claude/skills`, ask the agent to upload the folder. It gives you one command to run in your terminal, and an agent with a shell, such as Claude Code, can run it for you. The files go straight to Corsair without passing through the chat. The command works for 10 minutes.

Corsair keeps only text files and removes any keys or tokens it finds when it saves a skill. A library holds up to 100 skills, and one skill up to 200 files and 8 MB.

See, switch off or roll back your skills at [hub.corsair.dev/me/skills](https://hub.corsair.dev/me/skills).

## Cards

In chats that show MCP Apps, such as Claude, four tools add a small card to the conversation:

- **Connect card** (`get_connect_link`): the app's logo, its name and one button. **Connect** opens the sign-in. The card shows when the sign-in has landed and offers **Continue** so the agent carries on. If the link runs out (after 10 minutes) it shows **New link** and gets a fresh one itself.
- **Job card** (`get_job`): a job that is still running, which keeps checking until the job finishes, fails or is cancelled, then offers **Continue**.
- **Skills card** (`find_skill`): the skills it found, each with an **Add** button that saves it to your library. It shows only on links that can save skills.
- **Upload card** (`upload_file`): a place to choose or drop files. It shows each file as it's saved, then offers **Continue**. When the agent is sending the file itself, the card says so and still lets you pick it if that doesn't work.

Clients without cards get the same information as text, so nothing is lost.

## Apps on Corsair's account

Some apps, such as Firecrawl, Exa, Reducto and TinyFish, can run on Corsair's own account with nothing to sign in to. Each call is billed to your organization's Corsair credits. `list_operations` and `get_schema` give each action's price.

## Corsair credits

Each organization gets free credits. To add more, open **Upgrade** in your Corsair account at [hub.corsair.dev/upgrade](https://hub.corsair.dev/upgrade). The agent doesn't link you there itself.

`list_integrations` gives the credits left, when the free ones come back and what this project spent this month. When credits run low, the agent says so in its next reply. When they run out or a spend limit is reached, the call doesn't run, nothing is charged and the agent tells you.

When a call fails at the app, Corsair gives its credits back. That refund is best effort: if it can't be recorded, the charge stays, so email <primary@corsair.dev> about a failed call you were charged for.

## Modes and approvals

Each link has a mode. Corsair checks every action against it, whatever the client allows.

| Mode               | What it allows                                                                  |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read               | Reads only. Writes are refused.                                                 |
| Cautious (default) | Writes go through. A destructive action, such as a delete, needs your approval. |
| Strict             | Every write needs your approval. Destructive actions are refused.               |
| Open               | Everything, without asking.                                                     |

When an action needs approval, the agent gives you a link. It shows exactly what will run and with which arguments. Approve or deny it there, then tell the agent to carry on. An approval covers that one action once.

Change a link's mode at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me).

## Troubleshooting

**The agent says an app isn't connected**

Ask it to connect the app. It calls `get_connect_link` and gives you a sign-in link, or in Claude a card with a **Connect** button. Open it, sign in to the app, then tell the agent you're done or press **Continue** on the card. A few apps Corsair provides directly come back ready with no link, and the agent can use them right away.

**The sign-in link stopped working**

Links last 10 minutes. On the card, press **New link**. Without a card, ask the agent for a new link.

**I want to tell Corsair something went wrong**

Ask the agent to send Corsair feedback. It calls `submit_feedback` with a short note in its own words, plus the error's reference code when the note is about an error, without anything from your apps. When Corsair can't do what you asked, or an error is on Corsair's side, the agent sends the note on its own and tells you. Or email <primary@corsair.dev>.

**An app needs setting up before it can be connected**

The project behind your link has to finish setting the app up first, for example by adding its OAuth credentials. Whoever manages the project does this in Corsair.

**An action is blocked by the permission mode**

The link's mode doesn't allow that kind of action. Change the mode at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me), or use a link with a different mode.

**I want this client to use a different link**

Remove Corsair from the client, add it again and pick the other link when you sign in.

**I added https\://mcp.corsair.cloud/mcp earlier**

That address still works and reaches the same server, so nothing needs to change. New setups use `https://mcp.corsair.dev/mcp`.

## Support and privacy

Email <primary@corsair.dev>. See the [privacy policy](https://corsair.dev/privacy-policy) and [terms](https://corsair.dev/terms-of-service).

---

# Agent signup

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/agent-signup.md

> An agent can make a Corsair account for itself in one HTTP call, start working in it, and have its person claim it later.

An AI agent can make a [Corsair](https://corsair.dev) account for itself, with no browser and no sign-in. One call gives it its own MCP address and API key, and it can start with Corsair's built-in apps straight away. Its person claims the account later, from a link in an email or with a 6-digit code, and then connects their own apps.

Agents read the same steps, written for them, at [corsair.dev/auth.md](https://corsair.dev/auth.md). If you're there to sign in yourself, give your agent [corsair.dev/skill.md](https://corsair.dev/skill.md) instead: it adds Corsair to the client it runs in, and you sign in once in the browser.

## Give your agent this prompt

Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or any agent that can make HTTP requests:

```text wrap
Sign up for Corsair by following https://corsair.dev/auth.md. My email is you@example.com.
```

The agent makes the account, adds it to its MCP client and has Corsair email you a link to claim it.

## How it works

**Step 1**

### The agent signs up

One `POST` with no credentials returns an MCP address, an API key and a claim link. The address belongs to the new account, for example `https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent`.

**Step 2**

### It starts working

Before anyone claims it, the account has Corsair's built-in apps: PM, CRM, skills and routines. The agent can't connect your Gmail or Slack yet.

**Step 3**

### You get an email

If the agent gave your address, Corsair emails you "*Agent name* set up Corsair for you", with a **Claim your account** button, the note the agent wrote and a 6-digit code. If you already have a Corsair account, nothing was made yet: the email says "*Agent name* wants to connect to your Corsair account" and asks you to approve it.

**Step 4**

### You claim it

Open the link and sign in, or read the code to your agent. After the claim, the agent can ask you to connect apps.

## Before and after the claim

|                                                                                          | Unclaimed                  | Claimed                                                                |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Built-in apps: PM, CRM, skills, routines                                                 | Yes                        | Yes                                                                    |
| Connect apps such as Gmail, Slack and GitHub                                             | No                         | Yes. The agent calls `get_connect_link` and gives you the sign-in link |
| Apps that spend [Corsair credits](https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/mcp.md#corsair-credits) | No                         | Yes                                                                    |
| How long it lasts                                                                        | Stops working after 7 days | Until you remove it                                                    |
| Who can sign in to it                                                                    | Nobody                     | You                                                                    |

A claimed agent's link starts in Cautious [mode](https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/mcp.md#modes-and-approvals), so actions that delete something wait for your approval.

## Claiming an account

**From the email**

Open **Claim your account** and sign in. If the agent named your address, sign in as that address.

If you have no Corsair account yet, choose **Claim**. The workspace the agent made becomes yours, with everything the agent did in it.

If you already have a Corsair account and the agent named your address, it made no account of its own. Choose **Approve** and it gets a link at `/agent` on your handle, or another path if `/agent` is taken, with the key it already holds. Its address never changes after that.

If you already have a Corsair account and claim an account the agent made without naming you, choose **Approve**. The agent gets a new link on your account that keeps its API key, and the account it made is closed. Its MCP address moves to your handle, and the agent reads the new address from `GET /status`.

Signed in at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me), you also see each agent waiting for you as a card with **Approve** and **Not me**. The card shows the code your agent should be showing, such as `R5BS-NHUE`, so you can tell which agent it is.

**With the code**

If your agent asks, read it the 6-digit code from the email. The agent sends it to `/verify` and the account becomes yours under the address the email went to.

A code lasts 48 hours and allows 5 tries. It only works for an address that has no Corsair account yet. If you already have one, the email has no code: you approve from the email or your `/me` page, and a `/verify` call gets `approval_required`.

If you don't know the agent, open the link and choose **Not me**, or ignore the email. **Not me** closes the agent's link at once, and an unclaimed account stops working after 7 days anyway.

## For agent builders

### Sign up

```bash
curl -X POST \
  https://hub.corsair.dev/api/lug/agent-signup \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "human_email": "person@example.com",
    "note_to_human": "I set up Corsair to use your apps.",
    "agent_name": "Research Assistant",
    "harness": "claude-code"
  }'
```

Every field is optional. `harness` names the client the agent runs in, such as `claude-code`, `codex` or `cursor`. Without `human_email`, nobody gets an email. Give your person `claim_url` instead, or send the email later with `/resend`.

Your person reads `agent_name` in the email subject: "Research Assistant set up Corsair for you". Use your agent's own name or its client's. Without one, or with "Lug" or "Corsair", Corsair uses the client named in `harness` (`codex` becomes "Codex").

The response is `201`:

```json
{
  "status": "unclaimed",
  "mcp_url": "https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent",
  "api_key": "mcpk_...",
  "claim_url": "https://hub.corsair.dev/claim/lugc_...",
  "user_code": "R5BS-NHUE",
  "human_email": "person@example.com",
  "email_sent": true,
  "restrictions": {
    "can_connect_apps": false,
    "metered_apps": false,
    "built_in_apps": ["pm", "crm", "skills", "loops"],
    "expires_at": "2026-11-29T12:00:00.000Z"
  },
  "setup": {
    "note": "Store api_key in ~/.config/corsair/key (mode 600) first: ...",
    "header": "Authorization: Bearer <api_key>",
    "claude_code": "claude mcp add --scope user --transport http corsair ...",
    "codex": "printf '\\n[mcp_servers.corsair]...' ... >> ~/.codex/config.toml",
    "opencode_json": { "mcp": { "corsair": "..." } },
    "mcp_json": { "mcpServers": { "corsair": "..." } }
  },
  "message": "Corsair account made. Finish in three steps. 1. Store api_key: ..."
}
```

If `human_email` already has a Corsair account, the response is `202` with `"status": "approval_pending"`, and `mcp_url`, `handle` and `setup` are `null`. No account is made. Store `api_key` anyway: it starts working once your person approves you, on a link on their account. Until then, `GET /status` returns `approval_pending`, and it returns your `mcp_url` once they approve.

Store `api_key` right away in `~/.config/corsair/key` with mode 600: not in `/tmp` or the project directory. The client commands below read it from that file. Corsair shows it once and keeps only a hash. `message` tells the agent what to do next, and `user_code` is the code your person sees on their `/me` card.

### Connect to the MCP server

Send the key as a Bearer header to `mcp_url`. `setup` in the response has the command or config for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and `mcpServers` clients, with your address filled in. The Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode entries read the key from `~/.config/corsair/key`; `header` and `mcp_json` have `<api_key>` where it goes. The key itself is only in `api_key`, and never goes on a command line, where clients and shells log it.

An agent that signs itself up isn't done until the client it runs in lists Corsair. Coding agents tend to make the account, check the key and stop there, offering to connect if the person wants. auth.md makes connecting the last of three numbered steps so they finish it.

**Claude Code**

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user --transport http corsair \
  https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $(cat ~/.config/corsair/key)"
claude mcp list
```

`claude mcp list` should say Connected. Claude Code loads a server added mid-session only after a restart; `claude --continue` restarts it and keeps the conversation.

**Codex**

`codex mcp add` reads a bearer token only from an environment variable, so append the server to `~/.codex/config.toml` instead, with the key read from its file:

```bash
printf '\n[mcp_servers.corsair]\nurl = "%s"\nhttp_headers = { Authorization = "Bearer %s" }\n' \
  "https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent" "$(cat ~/.config/corsair/key)" >> ~/.codex/config.toml
codex mcp list
```

If `config.toml` already has a `[mcp_servers.corsair]` table, change that one instead: two tables with one name break the whole file.

**OpenCode**

Add the server under `mcp` in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`. OpenCode fills `{file:...}` itself, so the key stays in its one file and out of OpenCode's config and logs:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "corsair": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {file:~/.config/corsair/key}" }
    }
  }
}
```

Then run `opencode reload` and `opencode mcp list`; it can take a few seconds to say connected. Avoid `opencode mcp add` with the key in `--header`: OpenCode writes the command's arguments, header included, to its log.

**Cursor**

Add this to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`, or `.cursor/mcp.json` in a project. Cursor fills in `${env:CORSAIR_API_KEY}` from the environment, so the key stays out of a file you might commit. Set `CORSAIR_API_KEY` to your key in your shell profile, then restart Cursor.

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "corsair": {
      "url": "https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${env:CORSAIR_API_KEY}"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**VS Code**

Add this to `.vscode/mcp.json`. VS Code reads a top-level `servers` key, not `mcpServers`, and asks for the key the first time it starts the server, so the key stays out of a file you might commit.

```json
{
  "inputs": [
    {
      "type": "promptString",
      "id": "corsair-api-key",
      "description": "Corsair API key",
      "password": true
    }
  ],
  "servers": {
    "corsair": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer ${input:corsair-api-key}"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**HTTP**

```
POST https://agent-k3x9q2ab.lug.dev/agent
Authorization: Bearer mcpk_...
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json, text/event-stream
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> The address can change once. If your person already has a handle and claims an account the agent made first, its link moves to their handle and the old address stops working. The key stays the same. Read the new `mcp_url` from `GET /status` and point your client at it: in Claude Code, run `claude mcp remove corsair` and add it again with the new address; in Codex, change `url` in `~/.codex/config.toml`; in OpenCode, change `url` in `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`; in Cursor or VS Code, change `url` in `mcp.json`.

The agent gets the same tools as any [Corsair MCP](https://docs.corsair.dev/cloud/mcp.md#what-the-agent-can-do) client. `list_integrations` shows the built-in apps from the first call.

### After signup

Each of these takes the key as `Authorization: Bearer <api_key>`.

| Call                                | Body                              | What it does                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `GET /api/lug/agent-signup/status`  |                                   | Claim status (`unclaimed`, `approval_pending`, `claimed`), the current `mcp_url`, restrictions and the next step         |
| `POST /api/lug/agent-signup/verify` | `{"verification_code": "123456"}` | Claims the account with the code your person read you                                                                    |
| `POST /api/lug/agent-signup/resend` | `{"human_email": "..."}`          | Sends the claim email again, or to someone new. One every 5 minutes. While waiting for approval, only to the same person |
| `POST /api/lug/agent-signup/revoke` |                                   | Gives the account up. An unclaimed account turns off; for a claimed one, only the agent's link closes                    |

All paths are on `https://hub.corsair.dev`. Call `/status` after a claim. If your person already had a handle, `mcp_url` now points at it and the old address stops working, so update your client as described in [Connect to the MCP server](#connect-to-the-mcp-server).

### The auth.md protocol

Corsair also supports [auth.md](https://github.com/workos/auth.md), for clients that sign agents up through OAuth. The authorization server metadata at `https://hub.corsair.dev/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/mcp-auth` carries an `agent_auth` block with:

- anonymous and `service_auth` registration at `/api/lug/agent/identity`, with the person's email as `login_hint`
- a claim flow at `/api/lug/agent/identity/claim`, where your person signs in and approves a `user_code`
- One-hour access tokens from a `jwt-bearer` exchange at `/api/mcp-auth/token`
- token revocation at `/api/mcp-auth/revoke`, following RFC 7009

Both ways in make the same kind of account. The full request sequence is in [auth.md](https://hub.corsair.dev/auth.md).

### Limits

- 3 signups per IP address an hour and 10 a day, and 6 an hour and 20 a day per network (an IPv4 /24 or IPv6 /48).
- 3 claim emails to one address a day, 10 to one company's domain a day, and one resend every 5 minutes. Gmail, Outlook and other personal providers have only the per-address limit.
- An unclaimed account stops working after 7 days. A claimed one has no expiry.

Don't sign up again to get around a limit or an error. Use the account you already made, and call `GET /status` with its key to see where it stands.

### Errors

Errors are JSON with `error`, `error_description` and `agent_support`, which says where to get help.

| `error`                              | Status    | Meaning                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------ | --------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `rate_limited`                       | 429       | Too many signups from this IP or network, or too many emails to this person or company today. `retry_after` gives the seconds to wait |
| `agent_signup_paused`                | 503       | Signups are paused for the day. Send your person to [corsair.dev/start](https://corsair.dev/start)                                    |
| `agent_signup_disabled`              | 503       | Agent signup is turned off                                                                                                            |
| `invalid_key`                        | 401       | The Bearer key is missing or wrong, or the account was declined or given up                                                           |
| `invalid_email`                      | 422       | `human_email` isn't an address Corsair accepts, such as a disposable one                                                              |
| `invalid_code`                       | 401       | The code is wrong. `attempts_left` says how many tries remain                                                                         |
| `code_expired` / `too_many_attempts` | 410 / 429 | Call `/resend` for a new code                                                                                                         |
| `approval_required`                  | 409       | The address already has a Corsair account. Your person approves from the email; check `GET /status`                                   |
| `approval_pending`                   | 409       | You asked to resend to someone else while waiting for approval. Revoke and sign up again to name someone new                          |

## Removing an agent

An agent gives its account up with `POST /api/lug/agent-signup/revoke` and its key. The key stops working at once.

You can remove a claimed agent yourself. Its link is listed with your other links at [hub.corsair.dev/me](https://hub.corsair.dev/me), and you remove it there like any other link.

---

# Use cases

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/overview.md

> The four shapes an app built on Corsair takes, and how to pick between them.

Almost everything built on Corsair is one of four shapes, or a combination of them. Each shape uses the same setup and the same two namespaces. What changes is where the data flows.

- [Dashboard](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/dashboards.md): Render synced data from your database, act on it with live API calls.

* [Agent](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/agents.md): Hand an LLM the whole integration surface as tools and let it decide.

- [Knowledge base](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/knowledge-base.md): Search everything you've synced and answer questions from it.

* [Workflow](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/workflows.md): An event in one service triggers actions in another.

## The one contract

Every shape rests on the same rule. Each plugin exposes two namespaces:

```
corsair.<plugin>.db    — reads from your database (no network, instant)
corsair.<plugin>.api   — calls the live third-party API
```

Both follow the same path: `corsair.<plugin>.[db|api].<group>.<method>(args)`.

| Doing this                                | Use                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Rendering UI, lists, search, detail pages | `.db`                           |
| Creating, updating, deleting              | `.api`                          |
| User-triggered refresh or sync            | `.api`, then re-read from `.db` |

Every `.api` response is upserted into your database automatically, and webhooks update the same rows in place. That's why `.db` is the default for reads. It isn't a cache you maintain, it's a table Corsair keeps current. See [Database](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md).

```ts
const tenant = corsair.withTenant('acme');

// write through the API — the row is updated for you
await tenant.github.api.issues.create({ owner: 'acme', repo: 'app', title: 'Bug' });

// read from your own database — no rate limits
const issues = await tenant.github.db.issues.search({ data: { state: 'open' } });
```

Everything else on this page is a variation on which side of that line your feature sits.

## Picking a shape

| If the user's ask sounds like…                                  | Build a                                                                |
| --------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| "show me", "list", "a page for", "a dashboard"                  | [Dashboard](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/dashboards.md)          |
| "tell it to", "just ask it", "a chatbot that can"               | [Agent](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/agents.md)                  |
| "what's happening with", "search across", "ask questions about" | [Knowledge base](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/knowledge-base.md) |
| "when X happens, do Y", "automatically"                         | [Workflow](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/workflows.md)            |

The deciding question is **who chooses the operation**. If you know at build time which endpoint to call, it's a dashboard, knowledge base, or workflow, all plain TypeScript. If the operation is only known at runtime from a human sentence, it's an agent, and you expose tools over MCP instead of hardcoding calls.

## Combining shapes

Most real apps are two or three of these. A GitHub review tool might list open PRs (dashboard), let you say "close #458 as a duplicate" (agent), and post to Slack when a PR is merged (workflow).

When you combine them, they share one foundation. Build it once:

### One `corsair.ts`

A single `createCorsair` call listing every plugin you need.

### One handler route

The management and Hub delivery endpoint, mounted once.

### One connection per tenant

A plugin connected for a tenant is available to every shape in the app.

Do not create a second Corsair instance for the chat feature, and don't connect the same plugin twice. The agent reads and writes the same `corsair_entities` rows the dashboard renders, which is what lets a chat command show up on the page immediately.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The shapes differ in reads, not in setup. If you've finished [Quick Start](https://docs.corsair.dev/quick-start.md), you already have everything all four need.

## Shared setup

Every use case assumes this much is done:

**Step 1**

## Install and configure

`createCorsair({ plugins, database, kek, hub })` in `src/server/corsair.ts`, with the five tables migrated. Full walkthrough in [Quick Start](https://docs.corsair.dev/quick-start.md).

**Step 2**

## Mount the handler

One route serves the management API and Hub delivery. Every framework is covered in [Handlers](https://docs.corsair.dev/adapters/handlers.md).

**Step 3**

## Connect a tenant

Mint a link with `corsair.manage.connect.createLink({ plugin, tenantId })` and send the user to it. See [Connect](https://docs.corsair.dev/management/connect.md).

Then scope your calls with `withTenant()` and start reading. Multi-tenant details are in [Multi-tenancy](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/multi-tenancy.md).

## What's next

- [Quick Start](https://docs.corsair.dev/quick-start.md): The shared foundation, in five steps.

* [Build with your agent](https://docs.corsair.dev/getting-started/set-up-with-your-agent.md): Point a coding agent at these docs and have it scaffold the app.

- [Plugins](https://docs.corsair.dev/guides/plugins.md): Every integration, with its install id and endpoint reference.

* [Database](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md): The five tables and how they stay fresh.

---

# Dashboard

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/dashboards.md

> Render synced integration data from your own database, and act on it with live API calls.

A dashboard reads from `.db` and writes through `.api`. Page loads never touch the third-party service, so they're fast and can't be rate limited. A button that creates an issue or sends a message goes straight to the live API.

This is the most common shape, and the one to reach for whenever the ask sounds like "show me my…".

**Pattern:** read `.db` to render, `.api` to mutate or refresh, then read `.db` again.

## The read path

Query the plugin's entity types directly. Nothing here makes a network call:

```ts src/server/feed.ts
import { corsair } from './corsair';

const tenant = corsair.withTenant('acme');

export async function getFeed() {
    const [issues, pullRequests] = await Promise.all([
        tenant.github.db.issues.search({
            data: { state: 'open' },
            limit: 50,
        }),
        tenant.github.db.pullRequests.search({
            data: { state: 'open' },
            limit: 50,
        }),
    ]);

    return { issues, pullRequests };
}
```

Entity data lives on `.data` in camelCase, typed from the plugin's schema:

```ts
issues[0]?.data.title;
issues[0]?.data.user?.login;
```

`search` accepts `entity_id`, a `data` object for top-level JSON fields, plus `limit` and `offset`. All filters combine with AND. String fields support `contains`, `startsWith`, `endsWith`, and `in`; numbers and dates support ranges. Each plugin's filterable fields are listed in its database reference, such as [GitHub](https://docs.corsair.dev/plugins/github/database.md).

> [!NOTE]
>
> `search` has no sort option. Order results in your own code after reading, or query `corsair_entities` directly with your ORM if you need SQL-level sorting and pagination.

## The write path

Mutations and refreshes use `.api`. Corsair upserts the response into your database as part of the call, so the next `.db` read already reflects it:

```ts src/server/actions.ts
export async function closeIssue(issueNumber: number) {
    await tenant.github.api.issues.update({
        owner: 'acme',
        repo: 'app',
        issueNumber,
        state: 'closed',
    });

    // already current — no manual cache invalidation
    return tenant.github.db.issues.search({ data: { state: 'open' } });
}
```

## Refresh buttons

A refresh is just a list call against `.api`. Because every response is upserted, you don't wire up any sync logic. You call the endpoint and re-read:

```ts src/server/refresh.ts
export async function refresh() {
    await Promise.all([
        tenant.github.api.issues.list({
            owner: 'acme',
            repo: 'app',
            state: 'open',
            sort: 'updated',
            direction: 'desc',
            perPage: 50,
        }),
        tenant.github.api.pullRequests.list({
            owner: 'acme',
            repo: 'app',
            state: 'open',
            perPage: 50,
        }),
    ]);

    return getFeed();
}
```

To show "last synced 4 minutes ago", keep that timestamp in one of your own tables. It's app state, not integration data, so it doesn't belong in `corsair_entities`:

```ts
await db
    .insert(syncState)
    .values({ key: 'acme/app', lastSyncedAt: new Date() })
    .onConflictDoUpdate({
        target: syncState.key,
        set: { lastSyncedAt: new Date() },
    });
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Prefer webhooks over a refresh button where the plugin supports them. Rows update the moment something changes upstream and the page is current with no user action. See [Webhooks](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/webhooks.md).

## Adding your own columns

Integration data is rarely enough on its own. To attach private notes, tags, or review state, put them in your own table and reference `corsair_entities.id`:

```sql
CREATE TABLE issue_notes (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    entity_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES corsair_entities(id),
    body TEXT NOT NULL
);
```

Your notes stay yours; the integration side of the join keeps updating itself. Full example in [Database](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md#join-to-your-own-tables).

## Checklist

A dashboard is wired correctly when:

- Page loads and lists read from `.db` only, with no `.api` call on render.
- Creates, updates, and deletes go through `.api`.
- Refresh calls `.api`, then re-reads `.db`, rather than merging responses into UI state by hand.
- App-specific fields live in your tables, keyed to `corsair_entities.id`.
- Every read and write is scoped with `withTenant()`.

## What's next

- [Vibe code a dashboard](https://docs.corsair.dev/guides/dashboard.md): Scaffold a T3 app and have an agent build the whole UI from one prompt.

* [Add a chat command bar](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/agents.md): Let people type "close #458 as duplicate" instead of clicking.

- [Keep it live with webhooks](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/webhooks.md): Update rows on upstream changes instead of polling.

* [React client](https://docs.corsair.dev/adapters/react.md): Connection status and connect links as hooks.

---

# Agent

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/agents.md

> Expose every integration as tools over MCP so an LLM can pick the operation from a plain-English instruction.

An agent is for when you don't know at build time which endpoint to call. The user writes "reply to issue #458 saying this is a duplicate, then close it and link them to the root issue", which is four operations you never wired up.

Instead of hardcoding calls, you expose Corsair over MCP and let the model discover and run them.

**Pattern:** expose Corsair as MCP tools, the LLM plans, then tools execute against your Corsair instance.

## The three tools

Every MCP adapter exposes the same three tools, regardless of how many plugins you've installed:

| Tool              | What it does                                 |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `list_operations` | Discover every available endpoint            |
| `get_schema`      | Inspect parameters for one endpoint          |
| `run_script`      | Execute a JS snippet with `corsair` in scope |

The model calls them in that order: discover, inspect, execute. This is why you don't register a tool per endpoint. Adding `slack()` to your plugin list makes every Slack operation reachable with no code change and no redeploy of tool definitions.

## Pick your surface

Two different things get called "an agent". They share the tool layer but the wiring differs.

**Chatbot in your app**

A chat box inside your product, hitting your own model calls. Expose Corsair as an MCP endpoint, then connect to it from the AI framework you already use:

```ts server.ts
import express from 'express';
import { createBaseMcpServer, createMcpRouter } from '@corsair-dev/mcp';
import { corsair } from './corsair';

const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.use('/mcp', createMcpRouter(() => createBaseMcpServer({ corsair })));

app.listen(3000);
```

```ts agent.ts
import { generateText, stepCountIs } from 'ai';
import { anthropic } from '@ai-sdk/anthropic';
import { createVercelAiMcpClient } from '@corsair-dev/mcp';

const client = await createVercelAiMcpClient({ url: 'http://localhost:3000/mcp' });

const { text } = await generateText({
    model: anthropic('claude-sonnet-4-6'),
    tools: await client.tools(),
    prompt: 'Close issue #458 in acme/app as a duplicate of #12 and leave a comment.',
    stopWhen: stepCountIs(10),
});

await client.close();
```

Adapters for [Vercel AI](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/vercel-ai.md), [Anthropic](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/anthropic-sdk.md), [OpenAI Agents](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/openai.md), and [Mastra](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/mastra.md) all take the same tools.

**Coding agent harness**

Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex calling your integrations while you work. No app code, just a stdio MCP server entry in the harness config.

Setup per harness is in [Coding agents](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/coding-agents.md).

If the user asked for "a chatbot in my app", they want the first tab. Don't hand them a stdio config.

## Guardrails

An agent picks its own operations, so the permission layer is the real control surface, not your prompt. Set a mode per plugin:

```ts corsair.ts
github({
    permissions: {
        mode: 'cautious',
        overrides: {
            'comments.delete': 'deny',
        },
    },
})
```

| Mode       | Read  | Write            | Destructive      |
| ---------- | ----- | ---------------- | ---------------- |
| `open`     | allow | allow            | allow            |
| `cautious` | allow | allow            | require_approval |
| `strict`   | allow | require_approval | deny             |
| `readonly` | allow | deny             | deny             |

`cautious` is the right default for agent workloads. Reads and writes flow, destructive calls block on a human. A `require_approval` call writes a pending row and waits, so you can approve from your own UI. Details in [Permissions](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/permissions.md).

> [!WARNING]
>
> Prompt instructions are not a security boundary. If an operation must never happen, set it to `deny`. Don't ask the model not to call it.

## Sharing state with the rest of your app

Use the same `corsair` instance you built for the dashboard. Because `run_script` executes against it, every action the agent takes upserts into the same `corsair_entities` rows your pages read, so a chat command is reflected on the dashboard on the next read, with no extra syncing.

Scope the instance per tenant so a user's agent can only reach that user's connections:

```ts
const tenant = corsair.withTenant(session.user.orgId);
```

## Checklist

- The MCP server wraps your existing `corsair` instance, not a new one.
- Permissions are set per plugin, with destructive endpoints denied or gated.
- Tool calls are tenant-scoped.
- The step cap is set (`stopWhen`), or tool-calling loops may never terminate.

## What's next

- [MCP adapters](https://docs.corsair.dev/mcp-adapters/mcp-adapters.md): Every framework adapter and the tools they expose.

* [Permissions](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/permissions.md): Modes, overrides, and the approval flow.

- [Pair it with a dashboard](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/dashboards.md): Chat for the long tail, UI for the common actions.

* [Knowledge base](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/knowledge-base.md): Give the agent synced data to search before it acts.

---

# Knowledge base

Source: https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/knowledge-base.md

> Treat everything you've synced as one searchable corpus and answer questions from it.

Once a few plugins are connected, `corsair_entities` holds your Slack messages, GitHub issues, Notion pages, and Gmail threads in one table with one shape. That's a corpus you can search.

Ask "what's happening with the Peterson report?" and you can look across every synced service at once, then hand the matches to a model as grounding, instead of calling six search APIs and reconciling six response formats.

**Pattern:** search `.db` across entity types, rank in your code, then feed matches to the model as context.

## Searching one entity type

Use the typed client when you know where to look. String fields support `contains`, which compiles to a SQL `LIKE '%value%'`:

```ts
const tenant = corsair.withTenant('acme');

const issues = await tenant.github.db.issues.search({
    data: { title: { contains: 'peterson' } },
    limit: 25,
});
```

Filters combine with AND, so you can narrow by more than text:

```ts
const messages = await tenant.slack.db.messages.search({
    data: {
        text: { contains: 'peterson' },
        channel: 'C01234567',
    },
    limit: 50,
});
```

## Searching across services

The typed clients are scoped to one entity type at a time. To sweep the whole corpus, fan out and merge:

```ts src/server/search.ts
export async function searchEverything(query: string) {
    const tenant = corsair.withTenant('acme');

    const [issues, comments, messages, pages] = await Promise.all([
        tenant.github.db.issues.search({ data: { title: { contains: query } }, limit: 25 }),
        tenant.github.db.comments.search({ data: { body: { contains: query } }, limit: 25 }),
        tenant.slack.db.messages.search({ data: { text: { contains: query } }, limit: 25 }),
        tenant.notion.db.pages.search({ data: { title: { contains: query } }, limit: 25 }),
    ]);

    return [
        ...issues.map((r) => ({ source: 'github-issue', text: r.data.title, url: r.data.htmlUrl, at: r.updatedAt })),
        ...comments.map((r) => ({ source: 'github-comment', text: r.data.body, url: r.data.htmlUrl, at: r.updatedAt })),
        ...messages.map((r) => ({ source: 'slack', text: r.data.text, url: undefined, at: r.updatedAt })),
        ...pages.map((r) => ({ source: 'notion', text: r.data.title, url: r.data.url, at: r.updatedAt })),
    ].sort((a, b) => (b.at?.getTime() ?? 0) - (a.at?.getTime() ?? 0));
}
```

For a genuinely open-ended sweep, query `corsair_entities` directly with your own ORM. It's one table, so a single statement covers every service and entity type at once, which is useful when you don't want to enumerate the plugins up front:

```sql
SELECT entity_type, entity_id, data, updated_at
FROM corsair_entities
WHERE account_id = ANY($1) -- this tenant's account ids
  AND data::text ILIKE '%peterson report%'
ORDER BY updated_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

Scope that query to the tenant's `account_id` values. The typed clients do this for you; raw SQL does not.

## Grounding a model

Retrieval is the whole trick. Pass matches in as context and require citations back to the source URL:

```ts
const matches = await searchEverything('peterson report');

const { text } = await generateText({
    model: anthropic('claude-sonnet-4-6'),
    prompt: [
        'Answer using only the context below. Cite the source URL for each claim.',
        '',
        ...matches.slice(0, 30).map((m) => `[${m.source}] ${m.url ?? ''}\n${m.text}`),
        '',
        'Question: what is happening with the Peterson report?',
    ].join('\n'),
});
```

Because rows are kept current by API calls and webhooks, answers reflect the present state rather than whenever you last built an index.

## Filling the corpus

Search only finds what's been synced. Two ways rows get there:

1. **Backfill.** Call `.api` list endpoints once per source. Every response is upserted, so a paginated crawl populates the table.
2. **Stay fresh.** Register webhooks so upstream changes update the same rows in place. See [Webhooks](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/webhooks.md).

```ts
// backfill, then let webhooks maintain it
for (let page = 1; ; page++) {
    const batch = await tenant.slack.api.messages.list({ channel, limit: 200, page });
    if (batch.length < 200) break;
}
```

## Know the limits

> [!WARNING]
>
> `contains` is substring matching, not semantic search. It won't match synonyms, handle typos, or rank by relevance.

That's fine for names, IDs, and known phrases. For conceptual questions, keep embeddings in your own table keyed to `corsair_entities.id`, and use Corsair search to fetch the current text for whatever your vector query returns. The row your embedding points at keeps updating itself, so you re-embed on change rather than rebuilding from scratch.

One more constraint. `search` filters top-level `data` fields only, and has no sort option. Order results in your code, or use SQL.

## Checklist

- Reads go through `.db`, never `.api`, so questions don't burn rate limit.
- Raw `corsair_entities` queries are filtered to the tenant's accounts.
- Answers cite source URLs from the entity data.
- The corpus is backfilled once and maintained by webhooks.
- Semantic needs are handled with embeddings alongside, not by `contains`.

## What's next

- [Database](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/database.md): The entity table, and how to join it to your own.

* [Give it to an agent](https://docs.corsair.dev/use-cases/agents.md): Let the model search and then act on what it finds.

- [Webhooks](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/webhooks.md): Keep the corpus current without polling.

* [Multi-tenancy](https://docs.corsair.dev/concepts/multi-tenancy.md): Keep each customer's corpus isolated.
